title: Ndambe, Lamb and Black-Eyed Pea Stew on a Baguette
author: Binta Fall and Cherif Mbodji
desc: Cubed lamb braised with palm oil, tomato paste, paprika and black-eyed peas, cooked until the vegetables turn deep reddish-brown — spooned into a split baguette.
longDesc: Ndambe is the Dakar street-corner breakfast: black-eyed peas stewed with tomato and potato, ladled into a warm baguette so the juice glues the bread together. This is the Saveur printing by Binta Fall and Cherif Mbodji, made with lamb. Lamb is browned in red palm oil, onion, pepper, scallion and parsley cook to translucency, then tomato paste to a deep reddish-brown. Garlic, smoked paprika, vinegar, canned peas, bay and stock go in; lamb simmers uncovered until tender, a potato is added, covered, and cooked until it begins to break down. Quarters of baguette are split and filled.
ingredients: 10 oz boneless leg of lamb, cut into 1/2-inch cubes
1 medium red bell pepper, stemmed, seeded and finely chopped
3 3/4 cup drained, canned black-eyed peas, rinsed well (printed ‘cup’)
2 1/2 cups beef, chicken or vegetable stock
1 medium red potato, peeled and coarsely chopped
steps: Heat the palm oil in a Dutch oven. Brown the lamb until lightly browned all over, 2–4 minutes.
Add the onions, bell pepper, scallions, parsley, black pepper and salt. Cook until the onions are translucent, 2–4 minutes.
Add the tomato paste and cook until the vegetables soften and turn a deep reddish-brown, 10–12 minutes.
Add the garlic, paprika and vinegar, then the black-eyed peas, bay leaves and stock. Simmer uncovered until the lamb is tender, about 30–35 minutes.
Add the potato, cover, and cook on medium-low until the potatoes are soft and beginning to break down, 40–45 minutes. Season.
Split the baguette quarters, spoon the stew onto the bottom halves, close with the tops and serve hot.
chefTips: ‘A deep reddish-brown’ is the explicit colour target for the vegetables and tomato paste — wait for it.
The potato goes in late and breaks down; it is the thickener.
The warm baguette should be filled with a stew juicy enough to act as glue.
Lamb is the Saveur recipe’s choice; the companion feature calls lamb a variation on a usually meatless base.
commonMistakes: Stopping the tomato stage before the colour deepens.
Using a stale or cold baguette.
reheating: Gentle heat, covered, with a splash of stock.
healthBenefits: Black-eyed peas supply fibre, folate and plant protein.
culturalNote: ‘Ndambe, traditionally cooked for dinner, evolved to be served on baguettes for breakfast,’ writes Megan Zhang in the Saveur companion piece — the sandwich ‘started from the streets’, in Mbodji’s words, and Thiam recalls it as ‘something that was mostly for peasants’. The same article says there are as many recipes for ndambe as there are people who make it.
sources: Title as printed: ‘Ndambe (Senegalese Lamb and Black-Eyed Pea Stew)’. Byline exactly as printed: ‘By Binta Fall and Cherif Mbodji’. Publication: Saveur. Published 24 January 2023, updated 25 January 2023. Yield: ‘Serves 4’. Time as printed: 2 hours. TWO-PASS: pass one paraphrased, pass two returned the ingredient list verbatim; quantities agree on every item.

MINOR DISAGREEMENT between passes: pass one rendered the parsley as ‘1/2 cup chopped parsley leaves’ and the peas as ‘3 3/4 cups’; pass two (verbatim) reads ‘1/2 cup parsley leaves, finely chopped’ and ‘3 3/4 cup’. The printed form is ‘3 3/4 cup’, singular, confirmed by both passes. Pass one also reported a parenthetical on the palm oil offering vegetable oil as a less flavorful substitute; pass two’s list shows none. Both readings recorded.

Cues in short fragments: ‘until lightly browned all over, 2–4 minutes’; ‘until the onions are translucent’; ‘deep reddish-brown, 10–12 minutes’; ‘until the lamb is tender, about 30–35 minutes’; ‘beginning to break down, 40–45 minutes’. The method shape (browning order, uncovered then covered) is SINGLE-PASS.

Companion feature: ‘In Senegal, This Hearty Stew Doubles as a Delightful Breakfast Sandwich’ by Megan Zhang, Saveur, updated 25 January 2023 — the feature is by Zhang; the recipe is by Fall and Mbodji, and the feature quotes Mbodji and Pierre Thiam. SINGLE-PASS. The etymology of ‘ndambe’ is not given.

UNRECONCILED: the recipe uses lamb; the feature describes lamb as a variation on a base of peas, tomatoes and potatoes (‘some include okra, while others add meats like lamb’). A second named-author printing (International Cuisine) exists and was not fetched. Aïssatou Mbaye’s ‘Ndambé à la viande hachée’ (6 June 2020) is not published: no ingredient list and no soaking time.
